messages.content: Our storefront keeps showing the old price for a product after the warehouse team corrects it in the database. The database value is right — I checked. The page only catches up when we restart the app. What is actually happening?

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
Your program is fine and your database is fine — the memory in between them is lying. The first read copied the product into a cache, and every read after that is served from the copy. The warehouse team's correction updated the database through a path that never touches the cache, so the cache has no way to know its copy is dead. Restarting the app "fixes" it only because it empties the cache; the next read is forced to fetch the real value.

This is the stale-read pattern in its purest form: a write that bypasses the cache layer. There are only three families of fix. Make writes go through the cache layer so it can invalidate or update the entry (write-through). Give the entry a lifetime (TTL) so staleness is bounded instead of forever. Or publish an invalidation event on every write, including the warehouse tool's. What never works is hoping every present and future write path remembers to clean up — the bypass you found today is proof that one already forgot. Until you pick a fix, the honest status to give the warehouse team is: their edits are correct, and the storefront will lag them by up to a restart.

We added a 30-second TTL to our headline cache so it can't stay stale forever. Marketing still complains that after they edit the headline, the site shows the old one 'for ages'. 30 seconds doesn't feel like ages. Can you show me what readers actually experience?

arguments.code:
class Clock:
    def __init__(self): self.t = 0
    def advance(self, n): self.t += n

clock = Clock()
db = {"headline": "Spring sale ends Friday"}
cache = {}
TTL = 30

def get_headline():
    entry = cache.get("headline")
    if entry is None or clock.t - entry[1] >= TTL:
        cache["headline"] = (db["headline"], clock.t)
        return db["headline"] + "  [fresh fetch]"
    return entry[0] + "  [cache hit]"

print("t=0 :", get_headline())
db["headline"] = "Spring sale extended to Sunday"   # marketing edits at t=5
clock.advance(5)
print("t=5 :", get_headline(), "<- edit is live in the db")
clock.advance(24)
print("t=29:", get_headline())
clock.advance(1)
print("t=30:", get_headline(), "<- TTL expired at last")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
t=0 : Spring sale ends Friday  [fresh fetch]
t=5 : Spring sale ends Friday  [cache hit] <- edit is live in the db
t=29: Spring sale ends Friday  [cache hit]
t=30: Spring sale extended to Sunday  [fresh fetch] <- TTL expired at last

The TTL is doing exactly what it promised — the problem is what it promised. A TTL does not mean "readers see edits within 30 seconds of the edit." It means "a cached copy may live 30 seconds from the moment it was fetched." The edit landed at t=5, but the copy in the cache was fetched at t=0, so readers kept seeing the old headline until t=30 — 25 seconds after the edit, and if the edit had landed at t=1 it would have been 29 seconds.

Two consequences worth internalizing. First, the worst-case staleness is the full TTL measured from the last fetch before the edit, and the average is about half the TTL — so 'ages' is any TTL your users can perceive; for a headline, even 25 seconds of the wrong sale date is a real cost. Second, shortening the TTL trades staleness for load: every expiry is a fetch. If marketing needs edits to appear immediately, the correct fix is not a 1-second TTL (that's a cache in name only) but invalidating the headline key on the edit path, keeping the TTL purely as a safety net for writes that bypass it.

Users report seeing an old price after we update it. Before I change anything, how do I figure out WHERE the stale copy is living? We have a browser, a CDN, an app-level cache, and a database replica in the stack.

Prove staleness layer by layer, from the source of truth outward — never guess, because each layer has a different fix and fixing the wrong one changes nothing.

Start at the source: query the primary database directly. If the primary is wrong, this isn't a caching bug at all, it's a write bug. If the primary is right, move one layer out. Query the replica: if the replica lags, readers routed there see old data, and the tell is that staleness correlates with write load and heals itself in seconds. Next, bypass the app cache: call the data path with the cache disabled or from a fresh process. If a restart 'fixes' it, the stale copy lives in process memory — that restart test is the single most informative experiment you have. Then bypass the CDN with a cache-busting query string or a direct-to-origin request: if origin is fresh and the edge is stale, it's the CDN's TTL or a surrogate-key purge that never fired. Finally the browser: a hard reload or a private window separates your users' browser caches from everything you control.

Two pattern questions narrow it fast. Do ALL users see the stale value or only some? 'Some' points at a per-instance layer — one app server's memory, one CDN edge, one lagging replica. And does it heal on a timer? Healing at a suspiciously round interval is a TTL confessing. Write down the layer that fails the bypass test before you touch code; a fix aimed anywhere else is superstition.

A user upgrades to the pro plan, we update their record, but the app keeps treating them as free until the cache entry happens to expire. Our update code only writes to the database. Is the pattern itself wrong?

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
Yes — the pattern is the bug. What you have is write-around caching: writes go to the store, reads populate the cache, and the two never meet. The upgrade genuinely succeeded; the database says pro. But the cache is still holding the free-plan copy it fetched earlier, and it will keep serving it until expiry, because nothing in your write path ever told it the world changed.

The write-through version fixes it by making the write and the invalidation one operation: update the store, drop the cached copy, and the next read repopulates with the truth. (Updating the cached copy in place works too; invalidating is simpler and safer, since the next read rebuilds from the store.) The deeper lesson is that a cache is a second copy of your data, and every write path — this endpoint, the admin console, the billing webhook, the support team's script — has to participate in keeping it honest, or route around it deliberately. Audit your write paths, not just this one: the next stale-read bug is already sitting in whichever writer you forget.

We have a feature flag stored in the database. Support flips it in the admin panel, the database shows the new value immediately, but the app only picks it up when we restart. Is our admin panel broken?

Almost certainly not — the admin panel is writing correctly, and the restart behavior is the clue that convicts the real culprit. Your app is very likely reading the flag once, at startup, and keeping its own copy in memory. From then on it never looks at the database again, so the flag it acts on is a snapshot from boot time. The panel flips the truth; the app keeps consulting the photograph it took at startup.

Restarting 'fixes' it because a fresh boot takes a fresh photograph. That's the signature of a load-once config cache, and it's worth distinguishing from a write failure: if the panel were broken, the database wouldn't show the new value — but you verified it does.

Your options, in order of immediacy of effect: re-read the flag on each use (fine for low-traffic flags, and honest); poll it on a short TTL so changes land within a known window; or push changes with an invalidation signal — a message, a version counter the app checks cheaply, or an admin endpoint that tells running instances to reload. Whichever you choose, decide per flag: a flag that exists so you can kill a broken feature at 3 a.m. is worthless if it needs a deploy-shaped restart to take effect, so emergency flags deserve the most live mechanism you have.
Half our users see the new homepage headline and half see the old one, and it stays split like that for hours. A single cache with a TTL wouldn't do that, would it?

You're right to be suspicious — a single shared cache with a TTL produces a clean cutover: everyone stale, then everyone fresh at expiry. A persistent split means the stale copies live somewhere per-instance, and different users are being routed to different instances. The usual suspects:

Per-process caches. If each app server keeps its own in-memory cache and only some servers have fetched since the edit (or an invalidation only reached some of them), the load balancer decides which version a user sees. The tell: the same user can flip versions between requests if their routing changes, and each individual server is perfectly consistent with itself.

CDN edges. Each edge location caches independently and expires on its own clock; geography then predicts who sees what. A purge that reached most edges but not all produces exactly your symptom.

Database replicas with different lag. Normally lag is seconds, but a replica stuck behind a long transaction or a replication break can trail for hours while its sibling is current.

To separate them: hit each app server directly, bypassing the balancer, and compare; request through different CDN edges or with the edge location in the response headers; and query each replica for the value. The layer where the answer changes with the instance is your layer. And note the design lesson: in-memory per-process caches are the cheapest cache there is and the one most prone to this split-brain staleness — anything user-visible and edited needs a shared cache or an invalidation broadcast, not a fleet of private memories.

We cache stock counts with a 10-second TTL. Support says customers keep seeing wrong availability 'all the time', but 10 seconds sounds tiny. How much wrongness does a 10-second TTL actually produce under steady traffic?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
total reads:                                     40
reads served a value the db no longer held:      15

Fifteen of forty reads — 37.5% — served a number the database no longer held, from a 'tiny' 10-second TTL. Here's the arithmetic support is feeling. The sale at t=3 lands just after a fetch at t=0, so every read from t=3 to t=9 is stale: 7 reads. The entry refreshes at t=10, the restock lands at t=12, and reads t=12 through t=19 are stale again: 8 more.

The insight is that staleness isn't measured in seconds, it's measured in reads. Every read that arrives between a change and the next expiry gets the wrong answer, so on a busy key a short TTL still produces a large absolute number of wrong answers — and stock is the worst case, because the wrongness is actionable: customers order against a count that no longer exists.

If the business can tolerate 'approximately right, refreshes within 10 seconds,' this is fine and the TTL is doing its job. If a wrong count means an oversell, no TTL is short enough — the sale path itself must invalidate or decrement the cached count (write-through), reserving the TTL for the slow-changing display paths. Match the mechanism to the cost of one wrong read, not to how small the TTL number looks.
Should we invalidate cache entries with events when data changes, or just use TTLs everywhere? Events feel like more moving parts.

They are more moving parts, and sometimes worth it. The honest comparison:

TTL is a promise about maximum staleness with zero coordination. It never fails to fire, needs no plumbing, and works even when the writer is a batch job, another team, or a human in a SQL console — writers who will never publish your event. Its cost: staleness is routine, not exceptional, and every expiry is a refetch, so hot keys thunder.

Event-based invalidation gives freshness within milliseconds and lets entries live indefinitely between changes, which is a real load win for read-heavy, rarely-changing data. Its costs are structural: every write path must publish (the one that doesn't becomes your next stale-read bug), the event channel itself can drop or reorder messages, and 'the cache is stale because an event got lost' is a much nastier failure to debug than a TTL expiring.

The pattern that survives production is usually both: events for freshness on the paths you control, plus a TTL as a safety net sized to the worst staleness you can tolerate from the paths you don't. Decide per dataset by asking two questions: how wrong is a stale read (a headline vs a bank balance), and do I control every writer? Controlled writers plus expensive staleness argues for events; uncontrolled writers or cheap staleness argues for a plain TTL.
My tech lead says 'all caching is just accepting stale data, so stop worrying.' Is he right?

Half right, and the half he's missing is where the bugs live. Yes: any cache is a decision to serve a copy instead of the truth, so some staleness is the price of admission. But 'accepting stale data' is not one decision, it's three, and teams get hurt when they make them by accident instead of on purpose.

First: how stale? A 5-second TTL on a weather widget and an unbounded in-process copy of a user's permissions are both 'accepting stale data' in the way that a bicycle and a freight train are both vehicles. The window matters, and it should be chosen from the cost of a wrong answer, not from a default in a library.

Second: stale for whom, doing what? Showing yesterday's review count is cosmetic. Serving a revoked API key, a pre-upgrade plan, or a pre-correction price creates refunds, security holes, and support tickets. Read paths that gate money, access, or safety deserve invalidation, not shrugs.

Third: does it converge? TTL staleness heals itself. A write path that bypasses the cache, a key collision, a lost invalidation — those are stale forever, and they look identical to acceptable staleness from the user's chair. The professional version of your lead's point is: bound the staleness, price the wrongness, and make sure the system provably converges back to the truth. Worry about exactly those three things, and you can stop worrying about the rest.

We invalidated the shared cache correctly after a banner change — I watched the key disappear. Users STILL see the old banner. There must be another copy somewhere. How do I think about layered caches?

arguments.code:
db = {"banner": "Free shipping over $50"}
shared_cache = {}   # the shared cache ops invalidated
local_cache = {}    # a per-process dict in the app - invalidated by nothing

def read_banner():
    if "banner" not in local_cache:
        if "banner" not in shared_cache:
            shared_cache["banner"] = db["banner"]
        local_cache["banner"] = shared_cache["banner"]
    return local_cache["banner"]

print("first read:       ", read_banner())
db["banner"] = "Free shipping over $35"
shared_cache.pop("banner")     # ops invalidates the shared cache, correctly
print("database:         ", db["banner"])
print("shared cache now: ", shared_cache.get("banner", "<empty - would refetch>"))
print("reader still gets:", read_banner(), "<- the local layer never heard about it")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
first read:        Free shipping over $50
database:          Free shipping over $35
shared cache now:  <empty - would refetch>
reader still gets: Free shipping over $50 <- the local layer never heard about it

You invalidated correctly — one layer down. Real stacks cache in series: browser, CDN, shared cache, per-process memory, even a memoized function. A read is served by the FIRST layer that has a copy, and it never consults the layers behind it. Your readers are being served by the per-process dict, which fetched the old banner once and, having no TTL and no invalidation, will serve it until the process dies. The shared cache could be empty, correct, or on fire — the local layer neither knows nor cares.

Two rules follow. First, debugging: when a value survives a correct invalidation, don't re-invalidate harder — enumerate the layers between the user and the database and test each one by bypassing it. The layer whose bypass changes the answer is the one holding the copy. Second, design: every layer you add multiplies the invalidation problem, because freshness is now the minimum over all layers' behaviors. A local cache in front of a shared cache needs its own TTL or its own subscription to the same invalidation events; otherwise you've built a system whose effective TTL is 'until restart' no matter what the shared layer promises. Layers are added for speed one at a time and debugged as a stack — price them accordingly.
A customer from one company logged in and saw another company's admin name on their dashboard. Both companies are on our platform. Our user cache is keyed by user id. How is that even possible?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
acme's user 42:   {'name': 'Priya', 'role': 'admin'}
globex's user 42: {'name': 'Priya', 'role': 'admin'} <- asked for Tom the viewer

It's not only possible, it's inevitable with that key. User ids are unique within a tenant, not across your platform — both tenants legitimately have a user 42. The moment Acme's user 42 was fetched, the cache stored Priya's record under the key `user:42`. When Globex's user 42 arrived, the cache hit that same key and served Priya — name, and note the role: a viewer was handed an admin's record. A key collision is not just wrong data; where the cached object carries permissions, it's an authorization leak.

The rule is absolute: a cache key must contain every part of the identity of the thing cached — tenant, user, and anything else that scopes the record. `user:acme:42` and `user:globex:42` are different keys for different facts. Audit every key in the system against this rule, because the collision only fires when two tenants happen to mint the same local id, which means it hides in testing (one tenant) and detonates in production (many). And treat this incident as a security event, not a display bug: find out how many cross-tenant reads were served while the key was live.
How do I design a cache key properly? I keep getting bitten by keys that seemed fine when I wrote them.

A cache key is a claim: 'every request with this key deserves the same answer.' Design it by attacking that claim — list everything that could change the answer, and make sure each one is in the key.

Start with identity: whose data is it? Tenant, user, account — every scoping level, not just the innermost id. Then the request's real inputs: if the function takes five arguments and the result depends on all five, the key needs all five, including the quiet ones people forget — currency, locale, units, timezone, the caller's permissions, feature-flag state. Then the version of the answer's shape: when you change what the value means (a new field, a new formula), the old entries are wrong answers wearing the right key, so the key needs a schema or logic version you can bump.

Mechanically: build keys from structured parts (a tuple, or segments joined by a separator that cannot appear in the data), never from bare string concatenation of variable-length pieces, and normalize inputs first — trim, case-fold where case is insignificant — so equivalent requests share a key and different ones never do.

The review question that catches most bugs: 'Show me two different correct answers this key would merge into one.' If you can construct that pair, the key is wrong. Your past bites were almost certainly cases where the pair existed but nobody constructed it until production did.
Can a cache key really be too simple? It's just a string lookup.

Yes, and here's the scar tissue to prove it. Imagine a price cache keyed by SKU alone: `price:sku-100`. The US store fetches first and caches 89.99 — dollars, though the key doesn't say so. The EU store asks for the same SKU, hits the same key, and displays 89.99 with a euro symbol. Nothing malfunctioned. The lookup was fast, the value was faithfully stored and faithfully returned. The key simply merged two different questions — 'price in USD' and 'price in EUR' — into one, because currency changed the answer and wasn't in the key.

That's what 'too simple' means: not short, but incomplete. A key must encode the full identity of the question being answered. The failure mode is treacherous because it's silent and order-dependent — whichever variant is fetched first wins, and the other variant's users get plausible-looking wrong data. Plausible is the operative word: 89.99 in the wrong currency doesn't crash anything, doesn't trip an error monitor, and gets reported by a confused customer weeks later.

So when you review a key, don't ask 'is it unique?' — database ids are unique and still collide across tenants, currencies, and locales. Ask 'what varies that this key doesn't mention?' Every answer to that question is a collision waiting for traffic.

Our promotions lookup caches by store and aisle. Store 1, aisle 23 shows the right promo, but store 12, aisle 3 shows the SAME promo, and it's wrong for that aisle. The two lookups have nothing in common. What's going on?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
store 1,  aisle 23 -> ('123', 'Trail mix 20% off')
store 12, aisle 3  -> ('123', 'Trail mix 20% off') <- sunscreen aisle, trail-mix promo
the keys are identical: True

The two lookups have everything in common: the key `"123"`. Concatenating variable-length pieces without a boundary loses the information about where one piece ends and the next begins — `1|23` and `12|3` are different pairs that flatten to the same string. Whichever lookup ran first cached its promo under `"123"`, and the other has been reading it ever since.

Fixes, in increasing order of robustness. A separator (`f"{store}:{aisle}"`) works until a piece can itself contain the separator — store names with colons would reopen the hole. Length-prefixing each piece (`"2:12|1:3"`) is unambiguous for arbitrary data. Best in Python: don't flatten at all — use the tuple `(store, aisle)` as the dictionary key, since tuples preserve boundaries exactly and hash correctly. The general principle travels beyond caches: any time you serialize a composite identity into a single string — cache keys, filenames, idempotency keys, composite database keys in a text column — the encoding must be reversible. If you can't decode the key back into its parts unambiguously, two different things will eventually share it.
Following up on the cross-tenant cache leak: I changed the key to include the tenant. How do I prove the fix actually separates the two tenants' data instead of just believing it does?

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
Proved, not believed — and note what the proof consists of, because this is the shape of every collision regression test. First, both tenants fetch the same local id, 42, in the order that used to cause the leak: Acme first, then Globex. Each gets their own record — Tom is Tom again. Second, Acme fetches once more and still gets Priya, showing her entry wasn't clobbered by Globex's. Third, the cache itself is inspected: two distinct entries under two structured keys, `('user', 'acme', 42)` and `('user', 'globex', 42)`.

Two details make this fix trustworthy rather than hopeful. The key is a tuple, not a concatenated string, so the tenant/id boundary can never blur the way `'1'+'23'` and `'12'+'3'` do. And the test drives the exact interleaving that failed in production — same ids, colliding order — rather than testing each tenant in isolation, which is how the bug passed review in the first place. Keep this test. The next developer who 'simplifies' the key should meet it.
When people say 'cache key collision', do they mean a hash collision? Should I be worried about two keys hashing to the same bucket?

Almost never — and separating these two meanings will save you from worrying about the wrong one.

A hash collision is when two different keys produce the same hash value. Your cache implementation (a Python dict, Redis, Memcached) already handles that correctly: the hash narrows the search, then the actual keys are compared for equality, and different keys coexist in the same bucket without ever being confused. Cryptographic-grade accidental collisions are also astronomically rare with any modern hash. This is a solved problem that is not yours.

A key-design collision is when two different questions produce the same key string — user 42 of tenant Acme and user 42 of tenant Globex both becoming `user:42`, or store 1 aisle 23 and store 12 aisle 3 both becoming `"123"`. The cache is behaving perfectly; it's your key that asserted two different facts were the same fact. No hashing algorithm can save you, because the inputs were identical before hashing ever happened.

Every production 'key collision' incident you'll ever meet is the second kind: a missing tenant, a missing currency, a concatenation without boundaries, an input that changed the answer but never made it into the key. So spend zero worry on buckets and all of it on the question: can two different correct answers map to this key? That's a design review, not a cryptography review.
Our cache keys are built from whatever the user typed as a search term. Sometimes the same search misses the cache and recomputes. Is that a collision thing too?

It's the mirror image of a collision: not different questions merging into one key, but the same question fragmenting into many keys. If the key is the raw typed string, then `Shoes`, `shoes`, ` shoes `, and `shoes ` are four different keys for one search. Each fragment misses once, recomputes, and stores its own copy — so your hit rate sags, your cache fills with duplicates, and eviction pressure rises. No wrong answers, just wasted work, which is why it goes unnoticed longer than collisions do.

The fix is normalization at the moment you build the key: trim surrounding whitespace, collapse internal runs of spaces, and case-fold when case carries no meaning for the result. Two cautions. First, normalize the same way everywhere the key is built — if the read path trims and the invalidation path doesn't, you'll invalidate a key nobody reads. Second, only fold away differences that truly don't change the answer: case-folding a search term is safe; case-folding a key containing a case-sensitive token, filename on a case-sensitive filesystem, or a base64 blob would manufacture real collisions out of a performance tweak.

Rule of thumb: canonicalize the key so that meaning-equal inputs are byte-equal, and meaning-different inputs are guaranteed byte-different. Collisions violate the second half; your fragmentation violates the first.

We changed how a cached report is calculated — new formula, same report name. Now the cache serves a mix of old-formula and new-formula numbers depending on when each entry was created. How should we have handled that?

You've met the versioning half of key design: the key identified the report, but the meaning of the value changed underneath it. Entries written before the deploy are correct answers to a question nobody is asking anymore, and the cache can't tell them apart from new ones.

The clean fix is to make the key name the meaning, not just the report: `report:sales:v3` instead of `report:sales`. Deploying a formula change bumps the version segment; new code only ever reads and writes v3 keys, and the v2 entries become unreachable orphans that expire by TTL or get swept at leisure. No flush, no downtime, no mixed era — and rollback is free, because the old code's keys are still intact.

The alternative, flushing the whole cache at deploy, works but costs you a cold cache and a thundering herd of recomputation at the worst possible moment, and it fails silently if the flush only reaches some instances. A targeted purge of just the affected keys is fine when the set is small and enumerable.

Going forward, treat the version segment as part of the key from day one, even while it's `v1` and feels ceremonial. Any change that alters what a cached value means — formula, serialization format, the set of fields, the units — is a version bump. The entries you can't distinguish, you can't trust; versioning is how you keep them distinguishable.

Our search cache uses query objects as dictionary keys. Over a long session the cache grows but lookups start missing for searches that definitely ran before — and one user swears they got results for a completely different term. The query object is mutable. Is that a real problem or a ghost story?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
lookup Query('shoes'): <miss - entry orphaned>
lookup Query('hats'):  <miss> <- serves the SHOES results
entries stored in cache: 1

A real problem, and both of your users' symptoms are in this output. A dictionary key must never change its hash or equality after insertion, because the dict files the entry under the hash the key had at insert time. Your Query hashed as 'shoes' when it went in. After the mutation it hashes as 'hats' — but the entry still physically sits in the 'shoes' bucket.

The consequences are exactly what you described. Looking up 'shoes' computes the 'shoes' hash, checks equality against what's there — the stored key now claims to be 'hats', so equality fails: a miss, and a recompute, while the entry leaks in the dict forever (that's your growth with worsening hit rate). Looking up 'hats' is worse: it lands in the 'hats' bucket, finds the mutated key, equality says 'hats' == 'hats', and the caller is served 'results for shoes'. That's your user who got another term's results — not a collision between two keys, but one key that changed its identity mid-flight.

Fixes: make key objects immutable (frozen dataclasses, tuples, plain strings — the boring choices are boring for a reason), or snapshot the key material into an immutable form at cache time, e.g. key on `q.term` the string rather than on `q`. And add the review rule: anything used as a key must be immutable for the entry's whole lifetime, not just at the moment of insertion.
Give me a checklist I can use when reviewing someone's caching code — specifically for the key.

Six questions, in the order that finds bugs fastest:

1. Identity completeness. Can I name two different correct answers that this key would merge? Walk the scoping levels: tenant, account, user, role. Then the request inputs: every argument the underlying computation actually reads. The classic misses are tenant, currency, locale, and permissions.

2. Boundary safety. If the key is a string built from parts, can I decode it back unambiguously? Concatenated variable-length parts without separators or length prefixes fail this (`1`+`23` == `12`+`3`). Tuples and structured keys pass by construction.

3. Normalization. Are equivalent inputs made byte-identical before keying — case, whitespace, ordering of a set-like input — and is that normalization identical on the read, write, and invalidation paths?

4. Immutability. Is everything the key is built from immutable for the entry's lifetime? A mutable object as a key, or a key string built from a field someone can edit, will orphan entries and occasionally cross-wire them.

5. Versioning. Does the key carry a version for the value's meaning — formula, format, units — that the team actually bumps when the meaning changes?

6. Lifetime pairing. Does the key's granularity match the invalidation story? A key finer than anything you can invalidate (say, per-request timestamps) is unflushable; a key coarser than the data's variation (SKU without currency) is a collision.

A key that passes all six is doing its one job: guaranteeing that one key means exactly one question, forever.

We DO invalidate on write. I can see the delete happen in the logs. And yet, a few times a day, a just-updated profile goes back to showing the old value for hours. The invalidation works — so what else could resurrect the old value?

arguments.code:
db = {"profile:9": "name=Ana (old)"}
cache = {}
log = []

# a reader misses and starts a slow recompute (an expensive join, say)
log.append("reader: miss - starts recomputing from the db")
snapshot = db["profile:9"]            # the reader now holds the OLD value

# meanwhile the writer updates the db and invalidates, exactly as designed
db["profile:9"] = "name=Ana (new)"
cache.pop("profile:9", None)
log.append("writer: db updated, cache invalidated (nothing was there to delete)")

# the reader finally finishes and stores what it computed
cache["profile:9"] = snapshot
log.append("reader: finishes, stores its snapshot in the cache")

for line in log:
    print(line)
print("next read serves:", cache["profile:9"], "<- resurrected")
print("db truth:        ", db["profile:9"])

messages.content:
reader: miss - starts recomputing from the db
writer: db updated, cache invalidated (nothing was there to delete)
reader: finishes, stores its snapshot in the cache
next read serves: name=Ana (old) <- resurrected
db truth:         name=Ana (new)

Your invalidation works — it just fires into an empty room. This is the classic invalidation race, and it needs three ingredients: a cache miss, a recompute slow enough to straddle a write, and a store at the end. The reader missed and began recomputing from the old data. Your writer then did everything right — updated the database, deleted the key — but at that instant there was nothing in the cache to delete; the stale value was still in flight, in the reader's hands. A moment later the reader lands and stores its pre-write snapshot. The cache now holds a value that was invalidated before it existed, and with no TTL it can sit there for hours, exactly as you observe.

Notice why it's intermittent: the recompute has to be slow AND a write has to land inside that specific window. Expensive keys (joins, report fragments) race constantly; cheap keys almost never do.

Fixes that actually close the window: version-stamped stores, where the reader records the version it read and the store is rejected if the database has moved on (the next record shows this); compare-and-swap on store; or a short TTL as a backstop so a resurrected entry has a bounded life even if a race slips through. Deleting harder doesn't help. The delete was never the problem — the store was.

def store_if_current(key, value, version_seen):

    if version_seen != current:
        return f"rejected: snapshot is v{version_seen}, db is already v{current}"
    cache[key] = (value, version_seen)
    return "stored"

cache now: <empty - next read fetches the truth>

The stale store is refused, and the cache stays empty — which is the correct outcome, because an empty cache is just a future cache miss, while a stale entry is a lie with a long life.

The mechanism: every value in the store carries a version that increments on each write. A reader that misses and recomputes remembers the version its snapshot came from. At store time it compares: if the database is still at that version, nothing changed during the recompute and the store is safe. If the version has moved, the snapshot is provably out of date and is dropped. The next read fetches the current value and caches it cleanly.

Versions can be a counter column, an updated-at timestamp with enough resolution, or a hash of the value — the counter is cleanest because it can't tie or go backwards. The cost is one extra field and one comparison per store. What you get for it is the elimination of a whole race class without locks: writers never block, readers never block, and the worst case degrades to an extra miss instead of hours of resurrected data. Pair it with a TTL anyway — versions stop stale stores, but they don't help if a write path forgets to bump, and defense in depth is cheap here.
Explain the invalidation race to me in plain words. No code. Why doesn't 'delete the cache when the data changes' just work?

Because 'when the data changes' is not a moment — it's an interval, and other work happens inside it.

Picture the cache as a whiteboard in a hallway. A reader walks up, finds the board empty, and goes down to the archive to look up the answer. That trip takes a while — the answer needs a big lookup. While the reader is in the archive, a writer arrives with new information. The writer updates the archive, then checks the whiteboard to erase any outdated answer — the board is empty, nothing to erase, job done, writer leaves. Then the reader comes back from the archive carrying the answer they found — which is the old one, because they started their trip before the change — and helpfully writes it on the whiteboard. Now the board shows the old answer, freshly written, and it will stay there until someone erases it again. Nobody may come for hours.

Every element matters. If the reader's trip were instant, the writer's erase would land after the write to the board, and all would be well. If no write happened during the trip, the board gets the current answer. The bug needs the overlap: a slow fetch straddling a change. That's why it correlates with your most expensive queries and your busiest moments, and why it never reproduces when you test one request at a time.

'Delete on change' assumes the delete and the change are the last word. The race shows there's another speaker: the in-flight reader, who speaks last with the oldest information. The fixes all amount to making that last speaker check whether their news is still news before they write it on the board.

after W1's late store, cache: 100 <- the older job wins the cache
db truth:                   120

Because the database and the cache experienced the two jobs in opposite orders. In the database, W2's write landed after W1's read, so the database truth is 120. In the cache, W1's store landed after W2's store, so the cache holds W1's snapshot: 100. Each job honestly published the freshest value it knew — the problem is that 'when a job started' and 'when its store lands' are different times, and the cache naively applies last-store-wins to stores that were computed in the other order.

Any system where a value is read, transformed slowly, and then written back — caches, materialized views, search indexes, denormalized counters — has this hazard. The ordering guarantee you actually need is not 'last to store' but 'newest data wins.' Give each store a version or source timestamp and make the cache refuse a store that would move the entry backwards: W1's store carries 'computed from db state as of before W2's write' and gets rejected, or at minimum detected. Short of that, a TTL bounds the damage, and funneling both jobs' updates through the database with write-through caching (cache updated from the committed value, not from a job's private snapshot) removes the second timeline entirely. Two timelines, two truths — pick designs that keep only one.
Why can't I just update the database and delete the cache key in the same transaction? Then there'd be no race at all.

Because the cache is not in the transaction. A database transaction can make the row update atomic with other database changes, but the cache — Redis, Memcached, a process dict — is a separate system that knows nothing of your commit or rollback. Writing to both is a dual write: two systems, no shared atomicity, and every failure mode lives in the gap.

Walk the orders. Update the cache first, then the database: if the database transaction rolls back, the cache now holds a value that never existed. Update the database first, then the cache: if the process dies between commit and delete, the stale entry survives with no record that a delete was owed. Delete before the commit: a reader in that window repopulates from the still-old database. None of the orders is wrong exactly — each just leaves a different window, which is why experienced teams choose deliberately: the common pattern is update the database, then delete (not update) the cache after commit, accept the small window, and backstop with a TTL and, for expensive keys, version-checked stores.

If you need the gap closed further, the standard tool is the transactional outbox: record the intent to invalidate as a row inside the same database transaction, and let a separate process reliably publish those intents to the cache layer. The invalidation then inherits the transaction's atomicity for its existence — it can't be lost by a crash — though it still arrives a moment after commit, so the TTL backstop stays. Atomicity across systems isn't free; you buy it with a queue and a small delay, or you bound the window and move on.
I keep hearing 'compare-and-swap' as a fix for stale cache stores. Show me a minimal version working on the race where a sale lands while a reader is recomputing the stock count.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
reader tries to store its snapshot: refused: db has moved to v8
fresh snapshot stores:              stored
cache now holds:                    (35, 8)

Compare-and-swap turns the store into a conditional: 'put this value in only if the world is still the version I read it from.' The first reader's store fails the condition — it snapshot version 7, the database is at version 8 — so the stale 40 never enters the cache. The next reader snapshots version 8 and stores successfully. The cache ends with the truth, and nobody locked anything.

The swap comparison needs a version that changes on every write: a counter is ideal; a high-resolution updated-at can work if ties are impossible in your write rate. In a real cache you'd implement this with a tiny Lua script in Redis or a WATCH/MULTI transaction, so the check and the set are atomic on the server side — doing the check in client code and then setting reintroduces a (much smaller) race between your check and your set.

Compare this with the version-stamp approach: same idea, different enforcement point. Version stamps reject the store in your application logic; CAS pushes the condition into the store operation itself. Either beats the naive store. What neither fixes is a write path that updates the value without bumping the version — the version discipline is the actual contract, and it's worth a test of its own.
Rank the anti-staleness strategies for me. TTL only, invalidate on write, version stamps, write-through — when is each one enough?

From weakest guarantee to strongest, with the point where each stops being enough:

TTL only. Guarantee: staleness bounded by the TTL. Enough when the data changes rarely, wrongness is cheap, and writers are outside your control (third-party feeds, batch jobs you don't own). It stops being enough the moment a user can see their own change not take effect — people forgive a stale headline, not a stale profile they just saved.

Invalidate on write. Guarantee: fresh after any write that goes through your code, with small race windows. Enough for most application data where you control the write paths. It stops being enough when expensive recomputes race with writes (the resurrected-entry bug), or when some writers bypass your layer — imports, admin scripts, other services.

Version stamps / compare-and-swap stores. Guarantee: the cache can never move backwards; a stale store is rejected even under racing. Enough for high-traffic keys with slow recomputes and concurrent writers. It stops being enough only if the version itself can be bypassed — a write path that updates without bumping — which is a discipline problem, not a mechanism problem.

Write-through (cache updated synchronously from the committed write). Guarantee: the cache and store agree at every commit point. Enough — and appropriate — for small, hot, high-stakes data where reads vastly outnumber writes. Its cost is write latency and coupling: every write pays for the cache update, and a cache outage can block writes unless you design the fallback.

In practice you layer them: invalidate on write as the base, a TTL as the universal backstop, versions on the expensive keys, write-through reserved for the few datasets whose staleness would be a safety or money bug. The ranking matters less than matching the layer to the cost of one stale read.

Yes: stop treating the invalidation event as the only carrier of the news. In this design every cached entry carries the version of the data it was copied from, and a read cheaply compares the entry's version against the database's current version (a counter you can fetch with a trivial query, or keep in the cache itself as a version key the writer bumps). The lost event means the old entry is still physically present — but its version no longer matches, so the read treats it as a miss, refreshes, and answers correctly. The invalidation becomes an optimization (save the version check some work) instead of a load-bearing promise.

This is validate-on-read, and its tradeoff is explicit: you pay a small per-read cost — one light version lookup — to convert invalidation from at-most-once messaging into a correctness property. For most data that's a bargain. Just demote them: the system should be correct when they arrive and correct when they don't, merely slower. Any design where one lost message means a day of wrong data has a single point of failure wearing a queue's clothing.
Settle an argument: should we delete the cache key BEFORE updating the database, or AFTER? My teammate says before is safer because the delete can't be forgotten once the update succeeds.

After — and your teammate's instinct, while understandable, opens the worse window. Walk both orderings slowly.

Delete before update: the key is gone, then the database write happens. In between, any read misses, goes to the database — which still holds the OLD value, because your update hasn't landed — and repopulates the cache with it. Your update then commits, and the cache cheerfully serves the pre-update value it just fetched. You've rebuilt the stale entry yourself, after the delete. Worse, this window is as long as the database write takes, and it invites exactly the traffic the cache exists to absorb.

Delete after update: the write commits first, then the key is deleted. The window is the reverse: between commit and delete, reads may serve the previously cached value. That window is real but small and, crucially, nothing in it repopulates stale data — after the delete, the next read fetches the committed truth.

Your teammate's worry — 'the delete might be forgotten' — is about process crashes between commit and delete, which is a genuine failure mode, but the remedy isn't reordering; it's a backstop: a TTL so an orphaned entry dies on its own, or an outbox row written in the same transaction that guarantees the delete is eventually published. Ordering chooses which race you live with; backstops decide how long any race's damage can live. Delete after, add a TTL, and the argument is settled on evidence rather than taste.
Our test suite is thorough and it has NEVER caught one of these invalidation races. The bugs only show up in production. Are our tests just bad?

Your tests are probably fine at what they test — they're just structurally blind to this bug class. A race needs an interleaving: request A's steps and request B's steps woven together in one specific order. A normal test runs A to completion, then B to completion. That's one interleaving out of the many possible, and it's the one where the bug cannot occur. Running the same test a thousand times explores the same single schedule a thousand times.

Production explores other schedules for free, because it has concurrency, variable latency, and volume. The math is unforgiving: if the race window is the 50 ms of a slow recompute and the key is written once a minute under load, some reader will eventually be mid-recompute when a write lands. Rare per attempt, inevitable per month — which matches your 'a few times a day' far better than it matches any test run.

To test for races you have to manufacture the interleaving deterministically: pause the reader between its database read and its cache store (a test hook, a controllable fake, a barrier), run the write, then release the reader and assert on the final state. That's a different kind of test — a schedule test — and one per race-prone path is enough; you don't need them everywhere. Complement with the cheap production tripwires: a TTL backstop so any escaped race has bounded life, and occasional source-vs-cache comparison logging on hot keys, so the next resurrection is measured in your dashboards rather than reported by users.

The decorator didn't change your function's logic — it changed its contract. To memoize, `lru_cache` must use the arguments as a dictionary key, and dictionary keys must be hashable. A list is mutable, so Python refuses to hash it: `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`, raised before your function body ever runs. The crash is the cache lookup, not the sum.

This is a design signal, not an inconvenience. Hashability is Python's way of asking 'can this value serve as a stable identity?' A list can't, because it can change after being used as a key — and a key that changes breaks the cache exactly the way mutable key objects do. The fixes respect that signal: accept a tuple at the boundary (immutable, hashable, and it documents that the input is a fixed snapshot), or convert inside a thin wrapper. What not to do is hash a serialization of the list as a workaround without thinking — `tuple(prices)` is that, done honestly; a hand-rolled string join reintroduces boundary collisions.

The broader rule: memoization demands more of a function than correctness. Its inputs must be hashable, its outputs must depend only on those inputs, and it must be safe to skip executing it. The decorator checks none of that for you — it just starts crashing or, worse, silently serving history.

lru(maxsize=3), requests [1,2,3,4,1]: recomputed inputs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1] <- 1 was evicted by 4, so the repeat of 1 recomputed

Both behaviors are the same law from opposite ends: a cache's memory is proportional to how many distinct questions it remembers, and its hit rate depends on whether the remembered set matches the working set.

Your hand-rolled dict has no eviction at all, so every unique input is remembered forever. A thousand unique inputs, a thousand entries; a month of unique inputs, a memory graph that only climbs. An unbounded cache isn't a cache with infinite capacity — it's a memory leak with good intentions, and it also pins every argument and result object, keeping them alive past their natural lifetime.

The `lru_cache(maxsize=3)` run shows the opposite failure. The request pattern [1,2,3,4,1] has a working set of 4; a capacity of 3 means 4's arrival evicts 1 (the least recently used), so the repeat of 1 — the very hit the cache existed for — recomputes. When the working set exceeds capacity, LRU thrashes: near-zero hits at full memory cost.

So sizing is an empirical question about your traffic: how many distinct keys are actually hot in a window? Measure the working set (cache_info's currsize and hit rate over real traffic), set the bound above it, and always set a bound. 'Unbounded, we'll watch memory' is how day-long processes become week-long incidents.

Give me a straight rule: when is it actually safe to memoize a function?

Memoization is safe exactly when the function is a pure function of hashable arguments. Unpack that into a checklist you can apply in review:

Deterministic in its arguments. Same inputs, same output — not just usually, but by construction. If the answer can change while the arguments stand still, memoizing freezes one historical answer and serves it as current.

No hidden inputs. The function must not read anything that isn't in the key: no globals that mutate, no config, no clock, no random source, no database, no files. Hidden inputs are invisible to the cache key, so their changes are invisible too. (If a hidden input is unavoidable, promote it into the arguments — pass the config version, the rate, the date — and let it be part of the key.)

No side effects that matter. A memoized call may never execute on a hit. If the body also writes a log line someone audits, increments a counter, or sends a notification, caching silently deletes those effects on every hit.

Hashable, immutable inputs. Lists and dicts need converting to tuples/frozensets at the boundary; objects used as arguments must not mutate in ways that change their hash or equality.

Bounded working set. Even a pure function over an unbounded input space is a memory leak in a trench coat. Set a maxsize.

Fibonacci is the poster child because it passes all five trivially. Most production functions fail at least one — usually hidden inputs. The checklist's real value is that it tells you the fix when one fails: purify the function by passing the hidden input in, and memoize the pure core.

Because an `lru_cache` doesn't live in 'the app' — it lives in one process's memory. Each of your servers runs its own Python process (probably several workers per server), and each process has its own private cache, populated by its own traffic, cleared only by calls made inside that process. Your `cache_clear()` executed in exactly one process. Every other process kept serving its own stale copy, and the load balancer decided which users met the fixed process and which met the stale ones — which is also why reports were contradictory: the problem was genuinely fixed and genuinely present at the same time.

This is the per-process cache trap, and it shapes operations more than code. Invalidation of an in-process cache cannot be done from outside that process: an admin script, a management command, or a deploy hook that runs in a separate process clears its own cache, not the running servers'. Your real options: expose an authenticated endpoint on each running process that clears its cache, and call all of them; broadcast a 'generation number' through a shared store that each process checks cheaply and clears itself when it changes; or restart the fleet (which is why 'restart fixed it' is the folk remedy for this entire bug family).

The design lesson: in-process memoization is a per-process opinion about the world. The moment the data can change and the fleet has more than one process, you need either a shared cache, a broadcast invalidation, or a TTL short enough that the fleet converges on its own. Code being identical everywhere guarantees nothing — memory is where the difference lives.

They are equal (`1 == True == 1.0`) and they hash identically, so as far as any dict — including the one inside lru_cache — is concerned, there is only one key here. Whether this bites you depends on whether your function distinguishes values that Python considers equal. If `describe(True)` should say 'boolean' and `describe(1)` should say 'integer', a plain memo will serve whichever was asked first, to everyone — the same first-writer-wins shape as a key collision, one level down. Python's default equivalence merges 1, True, and 1.0 — if your domain's equivalence is finer than the language's, you must encode that in the key explicitly.
cache_clear() exists, so in an emergency I can just clear the cache and everything heals, right? Any reason not to?

It heals the staleness, yes — and then hands you a different incident to manage. Clearing a cache doesn't make the underlying data cheaper to compute; it makes every subsequent request pay full price simultaneously. If the cache was absorbing 95% of the load on an expensive query, a clear is a self-inflicted thundering herd: hundreds of requests miss at once, stampede the database or the downstream service, and can take down the thing the cache was protecting. More than one real outage has been 'we cleared the cache to fix the first outage.'

There are two more caveats. Process scope: `cache_clear()` clears the cache in the process that executes it. Run from a management shell, it clears the shell's cache and leaves your running servers untouched — the clear must be invoked inside each serving process, via an endpoint or a signal they honor. And completeness: clearing fixes entries that are wrong, but if the write path that created the staleness is still live, the cache refills with the same wrong values. Clear after you've fixed the cause, not instead of it.

If you must clear under load, do it surgically: clear the specific keys or the one memoized function that's wrong rather than the whole cache, and if the platform allows it, warm the hottest keys deliberately instead of letting traffic discover them. Treat a full clear the way you'd treat a restart — sometimes necessary, never free.
