Compute from source until you can prove you can't — storing an aggregate is buying performance with correctness risk, and the purchase should be justified by measurement, not habit.

Start with the honest cost of computing. A SUM or COUNT over an indexed column in a modern database handles millions of rows in tens of milliseconds. If your tables are thousands of rows and the query runs a few times a second, computing on read is simpler, always correct, and one less thing to drift. A surprising share of stored aggregates exist because someone imagined scale that never arrived.

Store when the computation is genuinely expensive relative to its read rate: aggregations over hundreds of millions of rows, joins across many tables, computations needed on every page render where 50 ms matters, or results consumed by systems that can't query the source (a static dashboard, an external API with rate limits). The tell is a measured latency or load problem with the compute-on-read version, not a feeling that a SUM 'must be slow.'

If you do store, you've signed up for the full maintenance contract, so price it in: increments must happen atomically with the source change (same transaction), every write path must participate (audit them, including imports and admin tools), edits and deletions of history must re-derive, and a periodic drift check must compare stored against recomputed so violations are detected by you rather than by users. Teams that store aggregates without the drift check aren't running a cache; they're running an unmonitored second source of truth.

The middle paths deserve mention: materialized views refreshed on a schedule (bounded, declared staleness), and database-maintained aggregates via triggers (the increment discipline enforced by the one layer no write path can bypass). Both trade a little freshness for a large reduction in the human promises that hand-maintained counters depend on.
I want to build a 'drift detector' — a job that catches stored aggregates disagreeing with their source rows. What should it actually do, and what do I do with its findings?

Build it as an auditor, not a fixer — its first job is trustworthy information.

What it does: on a schedule (nightly is typical; hourly for money), recompute each aggregate from source and compare with the stored value. Record every disagreement with the stored value, the recomputed value, the difference, and the time. Report deltas, not just failures: a drift of 1 on one account and a drift of 40% on another are different incidents wearing the same costume. Trend the count of drifted records — a system drifting more each week has an active bug feeding it, and the trend is your evidence.

What it must never do silently: auto-correct without a record. A detector that quietly overwrites stored values destroys the evidence you need to find the cause, and if the recompute itself has a bug, it will happily overwrite good values with bad ones across the whole table. Log first, alert a human, and make any auto-repair a separate, deliberate, well-logged step for aggregates whose source is unquestionably authoritative.

What you do with findings, in order: verify the detector (recompute one case by hand — detectors have bugs too, and a false alarm teaches the team to ignore the real ones). Quantify the blast radius: which records, since when (correlate the first drift timestamp with deploys and new write paths — drift onset is a fingerprint). Then hunt the cause among the writers: a path that skips the increment, a retry that double-applies, an edit that doesn't re-derive. The detector's trend line is your verification that the fix worked: drift incidents should stop appearing, not just be cleaned up.

One design note: make the detector's recompute path independent of the code that maintains the aggregate. If both share the same flawed helper, they'll agree with each other and both be wrong — the auditor must derive truth from the raw source rows by its own simple, obviously-correct logic.

We keep an append-only event log of everything that happens to an account, plus incrementally maintained totals. The totals have drifted twice this year. Someone proposed 'just rebuild the totals by replaying the log.' Why would replay succeed where increments failed?

Because replay and increments have opposite failure geometries. Incremental maintenance is a long chain of small promises: every event, exactly once, applied in order, by every code path, forever. Each link is a chance to miss one (a path that forgets), double one (a retry), or misorder one — and errors accumulate silently, because the total carries no memory of how it got there. After a year, the number is a sediment of every mistake the chain ever made, and none of them can be identified from the number itself.

Replay discards the sediment and re-derives the state from the log, which — being append-only and never edited — still contains the ground truth of what actually happened. The computation is a single, simple, testable fold over the events: start from zero, apply each event once, in recorded order. There's exactly one code path, it can be run in a test environment against the production log before anyone trusts it, and its result can be compared against the live totals to produce a precise drift report before you overwrite anything.

This is the deep appeal of event sourcing: state becomes a cache of the log, and like any cache it can be dropped and rebuilt. Your totals stop being a second source of truth and become what they always secretly were — a performance optimization over the log.

The caveats are real but manageable. Replay cost grows with log length, so large systems snapshot: store a verified state at a point in the log and replay only the tail after it. The event-application logic must be versioned carefully, since replaying a five-year-old event with today's code must produce what the event meant then. And replay only fixes totals whose inputs are fully in the log — if some changes bypassed the log itself, replay faithfully reproduces a world missing those changes, and you've found a different, worse bug. Given your history — two drifts in a year — the proposal is sound: rebuild by replay, then keep the drift detector running to prove the increments stay honest between rebuilds.
Design rule question: how do I make increments idempotent by construction, so retries and duplicate deliveries can't double-apply even if the code is sloppy elsewhere?

Four techniques, layered, each removing a class of sloppiness rather than relying on care.

Tie the increment to a unique event identity, enforced by the database. Every increment records the id of the event that caused it in a table with a uniqueness constraint, in the same transaction as the increment itself. A duplicate delivery tries to insert the same id, the constraint rejects the transaction, and the increment never lands. The database — the one component that can't be bypassed by a sloppy code path — becomes the guarantor. This is the strongest technique and the one to build on.

Make the increment a state transition, not an arithmetic operation. 'Decrement the member count' is repeatable and dangerous. 'Flip this row from active to deleted, and adjust the count only if the flip actually happened' can only take effect once, because the second attempt finds the row already deleted. Wherever a count tracks a set of things, anchor the adjustment to the thing's own one-way transition.

Prefer deriving from a set over maintaining a number. If the aggregate is 'how many distinct X did Y,' storing the set of X ids (or a row per X) and counting it is naturally idempotent — adding the same id twice changes nothing. Sets absorb duplicates; sums amplify them. Storage is cheaper than incidents.

Version the aggregate with its inputs. Store alongside the total the identity of the last event applied (or a high-water mark). An incoming event older than or equal to the mark is definitionally already counted and is dropped before any arithmetic happens. This also gives you ordering protection, which pure dedupe doesn't.

Notice what all four share: they move the exactly-once property out of the handler code — where retries, crashes, and future maintainers can break it — and into the data model, where it's enforced structurally. 'Be careful' is not a mechanism. A uniqueness constraint is.

Write up this incident the way you'd want to read it. Facts: shoppers kept seeing the $25 price for a product after merchandising set it to $19.99 in the admin tool. The database had $19.99 the whole time. The storefront uses a cache with no TTL; the admin tool writes to the database directly. It healed when we restarted. Give me the full forensic shape, with the proof executed.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
STEP 1 first read populates the cache: 25.0
STEP 2 source of truth (db):           19.99
STEP 3 what shoppers are served:       25.0
STEP 4 bypass test, cache dropped:     19.99

FORENSIC REPORT — stale price, sku-9.

Symptom: shoppers were served $25.00 after merchandising set $19.99; the discrepancy lasted from the admin save until the next application restart.

Staleness proven, not assumed: at the same moment, the source of truth held 19.99 (step 2) while the read path served 25.00 (step 3). Two values, one timestamp — the definition of a stale copy.

Layer isolated: dropping the cache made the very next read return 19.99 (step 4). The database, the network, and the rendering code are exonerated by that single test; the copy lived in the application cache, and only there.

Mechanism: the storefront's first read populated a cache entry with no TTL and no invalidation. The admin tool writes to the database directly — a write path that bypasses the cache layer entirely — so the entry had no way to learn of the change, and no lifetime after which it would die on its own. Restart healed it because restart is a cache flush.

Fix: route admin saves through the same layer as storefront writes so the key is invalidated on save, and add a TTL backstop so any future bypass degrades to bounded staleness instead of permanence.

Regression test: save a price through the admin path, then read through the storefront path and assert equality — the test must enter through the two real doors the incident used, or it will pass while the bug lives.

That shape — symptom, source-vs-served proof, layer isolation, mechanism, fix, regression — is the whole genre. Every section answers the question the previous one raises.

Do the forensic write-up in prose for this one: a Globex user saw Acme's admin name in his dashboard header. The user cache key was 'user:{id}' with no tenant. Both tenants have a user 42. Acme's user was fetched first that morning. Include the proof standard you'd apply and the fix.

FORENSIC REPORT — cross-tenant identity leak in the user cache.

Symptom: a Globex user (Tom, role: viewer) was shown the name of Acme's user 42 (Priya, role: admin) in his dashboard header.

Proof standard applied: a cache-collision claim requires showing that one key names two facts. Reproduction: fetch Acme's user 42, which populates the cache under the key `user:42` with Priya's record. Then fetch Globex's user 42. The cache answers from the existing entry — Tom's request never reaches the database — and returns Priya's record. Cache inspection confirms the mechanism: a single entry, `user:42`, where the system's design requires two. The deciding evidence is that reordering the fetches reverses the victim: fetch Globex first and Acme's admin sees Tom's name. A bug that follows fetch order is a key collision, not a data corruption — the database held both records correctly throughout.

Layer: the cache key construction, exclusively. Authentication worked (Tom was correctly identified as Globex's user 42); authorization data was then fetched through a key that discarded the tenant half of his identity.

Severity note: because the cached record carries the role field, this was not a cosmetic mix-up. Any code trusting the cached record's role would treat a viewer as an admin. The incident is classified as an authorization leak, and the exposure window is 'since the cache design shipped,' bounded by how often two tenants mint the same local user id — which is to say, constantly.

Fix: the key becomes the full identity — tenant and user id as structured parts (`('user', tenant, uid)`), never a bare local id. Regression test: the exact interleaving above, both orders, asserting each tenant receives only its own record. Audit: every cache key in the system reviewed against the rule 'the key must contain every part of the identity of the thing cached,' because this defect pattern rarely exists in only one place.
Before I let anyone 'fix' a staleness bug on my team, I want a method they must follow. What's the forensic discipline for caching bugs, in order?

Five steps, in order, and the order is the discipline — each step prevents a classic way these investigations go wrong.

1. Prove staleness before theorizing. Capture the source value and the served value at the same moment and put them side by side. If you can't produce that pair, you don't yet have a caching bug — you have a report of one, which might be a write bug, a rendering bug, or a user looking at a screenshot from yesterday. Half of all 'cache bugs' die at this step, correctly.

2. Enumerate the layers, then bisect them. List every copy between the database and the user's eye: browser, CDN, shared cache, process memory, memoized functions, replicas, derived tables. Then bypass layers one at a time — fresh process, cache-busting request, direct replica query — until bypassing one changes the answer. That layer holds the copy. Never guess the layer from the symptom; identical symptoms are produced by every layer.

3. Find the mechanism inside the layer. Now that you know where, determine why the copy is wrong: a write that bypassed it, a key that merged two facts, a race that resurrected it, a TTL that hadn't run out, an invalidation that reached one instance of many. Each mechanism has a different fix, and 'the cache was stale' is not a mechanism.

4. Quantify the window and the blast radius. When did the copy diverge, when did it converge (or will it), and how many reads were served from it? This turns 'users saw wrong data' into an incident record, and it's what support needs to answer 'was I affected?'

5. Fix the mechanism, then write the regression test through the real paths. The test must write through the door the incident used and read through the door the victim used. A test of the cache class in isolation would have passed before, during, and after almost every incident in this family.

Teams that skip to step 5 ship fixes for layers that weren't broken and mechanisms that weren't the cause — and meet the same bug again wearing a different key.

Forensic write-up, prose version: our dashboard order count drifted below the real number of orders over about six weeks. The count is a stored counter incremented by the order service. Three months ago a bulk-import tool was added that inserts orders directly. Recompute shows the gap equals exactly the number of imported orders. Give me the report.

FORENSIC REPORT — order-count drift via an unincremented write path.

Symptom: the dashboard's order count fell progressively behind the true number of orders over six weeks, with the gap growing in steps rather than smoothly.

Staleness — here, drift — proven: a full recompute from the orders table was compared against the stored counter. The stored value was lower, and the difference equaled, to the unit, the number of orders inserted by the bulk-import tool since its introduction. An exact match between the drift and one write path's volume is as close to a signature as this bug class produces.

Layer: the derived counter itself — or more precisely, the maintenance protocol around it. The counter was never computed; it was incremented, by convention, in the order service's insert path. The import tool inserts orders through the database directly and had no knowledge of the convention. Every path that creates an order is a maintainer of the counter, whether it knows it or not; this one didn't know.

Mechanism: not a race, not a TTL, not a lost message — a missing increment, repeated deterministically once per imported order. That explains the stepwise growth: the gap widened on import days and stayed flat between them, a pattern visible in hindsight in the monitoring graph.

Fix, in three parts. Correct the value by recompute. Make the increment structural: move it into the single insert routine (or a database trigger) that every path, including the importer, must pass through — conventions that live in documentation get bypassed by the next tool; conventions that live in the only doorway don't. Add a scheduled drift check comparing stored vs recomputed counts, alerting on any nonzero difference, so a future path that finds a new doorway is caught within a day.

Regression evidence: after the fix, a test import of known size leaves the counter exact, and the drift check has reported zero for two consecutive weeks. Closing note for the team: audit every other stored counter in the system for the same exposure — a counter maintained by convention is a bug that hasn't met its second write path yet.

Incident to reconstruct: our auth service was down for about 40 seconds at 09:00. Some users were told 'access denied' during it — fair enough — but the SAME users kept being denied until 10:00, long after auth recovered. Our authorization results are cached for 3600 seconds. Reconstruct it with the proof executed.

auth_up = {"v": False}          # 09:00 - the auth service is down
cache = {}
now = 0
TTL = 3600

def authorize(user):
    e = cache.get(user)
    if e is not None and now - e[1] < TTL:
        return e[0]
    if not auth_up["v"]:
        decision = "denied (auth service unreachable)"
    else:
        decision = "allowed"
    cache[user] = (decision, now)     # whatever happened gets cached for an hour
    return decision

print("t=0    during the outage, lee is told:  ", authorize("lee"))
auth_up["v"] = True                   # 09:00:40 - auth service recovers
now = 300
print("t=300  auth healthy for 5 minutes, lee: ", authorize("lee"))
now = 3600
print("t=3600 the cached entry expires, lee:   ", authorize("lee"))

messages.content:
t=0    during the outage, lee is told:   denied (auth service unreachable)
t=300  auth healthy for 5 minutes, lee:  denied (auth service unreachable)
t=3600 the cached entry expires, lee:    allowed

FORENSIC REPORT — an outage cached as a denial.

Symptom: a subset of users received 'access denied' continuously from 09:00 to 10:00, while the auth service was down only from 09:00:00 to 09:00:40.

Reconstruction: a user who attempted access during the 40-second outage got a decision manufactured by the failure itself — the auth service never evaluated them; it was unreachable. That non-decision was written into the authorization cache with the standard 3600-second TTL (t=0). From then on, the cache answered on the auth service's behalf: at t=300, five minutes after full recovery, the user is still denied, because no request in that hour ever reaches the healthy service. At t=3600 the entry expires, the next request is evaluated for real, and access returns — which is why the incident 'healed itself' at a suspiciously round time.

Mechanism: an error was cached as if it were a negative result. 'The authority said no' and 'the authority could not be asked' are opposite kinds of information; the code stored both in the same slot with the same lifetime. The blast radius follows automatically: exactly the users who tried during 40 seconds were locked out for an hour — a 90× amplification of the original outage.

Fix: authorization cache writes happen only on a completed evaluation, with the outcome recorded as allow or deny; transport failures are never cached and surface to the user as 'temporarily unavailable,' not 'denied.' If product insists on caching denials at all, their TTL belongs in seconds. Regression test: simulate the auth dependency failing for one call, restore it, and assert the very next request is evaluated fresh. The incident's lesson generalizes: a cache must never store the output of a dependency that didn't answer.
You keep saying the regression test for a caching bug must 'read like a user.' What does that actually mean in practice, and why do our normal unit tests keep missing these bugs?

A test reads like a user when it enters and exits through the same doors the incident did: the real write path and the real read path, in the order and combination that failed. Concretely, for a stale-price bug, the test is not 'put a value in the cache, change the database, assert the cache is stale' — that test documents the bug and passes forever. The test is: save a price through the admin tool's code path, then fetch it through the storefront's read path, and assert the shopper sees the new price. For a key collision: fetch tenant A's record, then tenant B's same-id record, through the real service function, and assert B gets B's data. For a race: hold the reader between its database read and its cache store, run the write, release, and assert the final served value.

Your unit tests miss these bugs for structural reasons. They test the cache class in isolation, where the cache behaves exactly as specified — the bugs live in the interactions the isolation removes: the write path that bypassed the layer, the key built three files away, the interleaving no sequential test performs. They also test components in the order the developer imagined, while incidents arrive in the order production invents.

This doesn't mean more integration tests for everything. It means one incident-shaped test per caching incident, kept forever, named after the failure ('test_admin_save_is_visible_on_storefront', 'test_tenant_isolation_same_user_id'). These tests are the institutional memory of the ways your system has actually lied. A cache with ten such tests around it is a cache whose known lies are all dead; the unit tests can then do their proper job of keeping the mechanics honest.

I'm writing the postmortem for a stale-data incident and my draft says 'a minor caching issue caused some users to briefly see slightly outdated information.' My manager says that's weasel wording. What should an honest caching postmortem actually state?

Your manager is right — that sentence is engineered to minimize, and readers can tell. 'Minor' is a conclusion you're asking them to accept, 'some users' hides a number you should know, 'briefly' hides a duration you should state, and 'slightly outdated' hides how wrong the data was. An honest postmortem replaces every softener with a measurement:

Name the layer and mechanism, precisely: 'The storefront's application cache held product prices with no TTL and no invalidation. Prices updated through the admin tool write directly to the database, bypassing the cache, so the storefront served pre-update prices.' A reader should be able to find the bug from your description.

State the window with timestamps: 'From 14:02, when the price was corrected, until 15:37, when the service was restarted.' If the window ended by expiry or restart rather than by your fix, say so.

Quantify the blast radius: how many reads were served stale, how many distinct users or products, and what the wrong values were versus the right ones. '412 product-page reads across 38 products showed the old price; the largest discrepancy was $30 on one item.' If you can't quantify it, say that and say why — an admitted unknown is honest; a vague adjective is not.

State the consequence plainly, including the uncomfortable parts: whether anyone bought at the wrong price, what you did about those orders, and whether the same defect pattern exists elsewhere (you should have checked before writing this).

Close with the fix and the regression test, named concretely. The test of the whole document: could a reader reconstruct the incident, judge its severity themselves, and verify your fix addresses the mechanism? If yes, you don't need the word 'minor' — the facts will calibrate the reader better than your adjectives ever will, in either direction.

instance_a = {}      # process A's private in-memory cache
instance_b = {}      # process B's private in-memory cache

def read(inst):
    if "promo" not in inst:
        inst["promo"] = db["promo"]
    return inst["promo"]

print("both instances warmed:        ", read(instance_a), "/", read(instance_b))
db["promo"] = "20% off"
instance_a.clear()   # the invalidation call reached instance A only
print("request 1 (routed to A):      ", read(instance_a))
print("request 2 (routed to B):      ", read(instance_b), "<- same user, one refresh later")

request 1 (routed to A):       20% off
request 2 (routed to B):       10% off <- same user, one refresh later

FORENSIC REPORT — the flickering banner.

Symptom: after a promo update, consecutive refreshes alternate between the new and old banner, indefinitely.

Reconstruction: both instances warmed their private caches with '10% off'. The promo was updated in the database, and the invalidation was called — once. An invalidation endpoint executes in exactly one process; it cleared instance A's cache. Instance B was never told, and B's in-memory entry has no TTL, so B will serve '10% off' until the process restarts. The load balancer routes the user's refreshes between the two: A (post-invalidation) fetches and serves '20% off'; B serves its preserved '10% off'; A again, new; B again, old. The flicker is not instability in any component — it's two stable, disagreeing copies behind one hostname.

Proof standard: the alternation itself is the fingerprint. A single stale cache converges monotonically (stale, then fresh forever). A value that oscillates per-request requires at least two serving copies in different states, and the oscillation period matches request routing, not any timer.

Fix options, by increasing strength: give in-process entries a TTL so B converges on its own within a bounded window; broadcast invalidations to all instances (a pub/sub message each process subscribes to); move the banner to the shared cache so there is one copy to invalidate; or version-check on read against a shared counter. What does not fix it: calling the invalidation endpoint 'again' — it will land on whichever instance the balancer chooses and clear that one, again.

Process note: any operational action aimed at 'the cache' in a fleet of processes is aimed at a fiction. There are N caches. Tooling and runbooks should say which instances were invalidated and verify each one — or the flicker becomes the teacher.

Capstone question. Give me the complete forensic checklist for ANY 'the data is wrong but the code looks right' report — the questions, in order, that you'd work through before allowing a fix. Assume caching or derived state is suspected but not proven.

Work these in order; each stage either resolves the case or earns the next.

STAGE 1 — ESTABLISH THE FACTS. (1) What exact value was served, to whom, when? Get the literal wrong value, not a paraphrase. (2) What does the source of truth hold right now, and what did it hold at that moment (audit log, history table, binlog)? (3) Can you produce source and served values for the same instant? If not, stop: you have a report, not a bug, and the next step is instrumentation, not fixing.

STAGE 2 — FIND THE COPY. (4) Enumerate every copy of this data between source and eyeball: browser, CDN, shared cache, per-process memory, memoized functions, read replicas, search indexes, derived tables, stored aggregates. (5) Bypass them one at a time — fresh process, cache-busting URL, direct primary query, replica-by-replica — until one bypass changes the answer. That layer holds the stale copy. (6) If no bypass changes it, the source itself was wrong at read time: this is a write-path bug wearing a cache costume. Redirect the investigation.

STAGE 3 — FIND THE MECHANISM. Within the guilty layer, which of the canonical mechanisms? (7) Did any write path bypass the layer (imports, admin tools, other services, direct SQL)? (8) Does the key merge two facts (missing tenant/scope/version, concatenation collisions, equality quirks like 1 == True)? (9) Could an in-flight reader have resurrected it (slow recompute straddling a write)? (10) Is an invalidation missing some instances, or was an error/absence cached as if it were data? (11) For derived state: which writer skips the increment, or double-applies it, and can an edit to history invalidate a suffix?

STAGE 4 — QUANTIFY. (12) When did divergence begin — correlate with deploys, new write paths, traffic changes. (13) How many reads were served from the bad copy, to how many users, with what consequences (money, access, trust)? (14) Is it still diverging now?

STAGE 5 — FIX AND PROVE. (15) Fix the mechanism, not the symptom: route the bypassing write through the layer, complete the key, version the store, uncache the error. (16) Write the regression test through the incident's real entry and exit paths, including the interleaving if there was one. (17) Add detection — a drift/staleness check comparing source to served on a schedule — because a mechanism found once exists elsewhere. (18) Write the postmortem with measurements, not adjectives.

The checklist's real function is discipline under pressure: the urge in every stale-data incident is to restart, flush, and move on. That urge destroys the evidence, leaves the mechanism armed, and guarantees a sequel. Work the stages; the fix is the short part at the end.

Last forensic write-up, prose: a user opened their cart and saw items they never added — items that belonged to another user active at the same time. The cart is kept in a module-level dict keyed by 'current session', but the session id is stored in a single global variable set at login. The other user's login interleaved with the first user's browsing. Give me the report: mechanism, proof standard, fix, regression test.

FORENSIC REPORT — cart contents crossed between concurrent users.

Symptom: user A viewed a cart containing items added by user B. Both users were active in overlapping windows. No database records were crossed — each user's stored cart in the database was correct throughout.

Mechanism: the design held two pieces of state with mismatched scopes. The carts lived in a module-level dict, keyed by session id — a structure capable of holding many users' carts correctly. But the session id itself was kept in a single global variable, set at login. 'Current session' is a per-request fact stored in a per-process slot. When B logged in while A's requests were in flight, the global flipped to B's session id. A's subsequent cart reads and writes were then keyed by B's session: A saw B's cart, and worse, A's additions during the window were written into B's cart. The dict was fine; the pointer to 'whose dict entry' was shared by the whole process.

Proof standard: state bleed is proven by interleaving, not by inspection. The reproduction drives the exact schedule: A logs in (global = A), A adds an item, B logs in (global = B), A reads the cart. If A is served B's cart, the mechanism is confirmed — and crucially, the sequential version of the same steps (A's full session, then B's) passes, which explains why all pre-production testing missed it and why the incident required simultaneous activity. The database's correctness throughout isolates the fault to the in-process layer.

Severity: beyond the confusion, any write A made during the window landed in B's cart, and cart contents can carry information (sizes, addresses at checkout, gift messages). Treat as a privacy incident; determine from logs how many sessions overlapped on shared processes during the exposure window.

Fix: abolish the global. The session id must travel with the request — read from the request's own cookie/token at each use, or held in request-scoped context (framework request object or contextvars) set by middleware from the request itself. There must be no moment where 'whose session' is a question the process answers from memory. Audit follows: every module-level variable that names a principal — current user, current tenant, current anything — is this same bug awaiting an interleaving.

Regression test: the interleaved schedule itself, automated — begin A, begin B, assert A's view contains only A's items, and assert A's writes during the overlap land in A's cart. Sequential tests are explicitly insufficient for this class and the test's name should say why it exists: test_interleaved_sessions_do_not_cross.
